## Word Problems
Derivatives are just the change in x / change in f'(x)?. Just rate of change for word problems

If you find the rate of change of a function (derivative), you can estimate the value of the function just about anywhere if you do (desired value / a known value) and multiply it by the rate of change
If you have a function that’s unit is the total cost of something given an equation, the derivative is cost per unit

The input of f(x) is the same as the input of f'(x)

When thinking of word problems, it is most helpful to think of derivatives in alternative df/dx notation. It helps remind you that the application of it is units of y per unit of x or units of output per unit of input

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Note: If the slope of f(x) is negative, then the graph of f'(x) will be below the x-axis
If the slope of f(x) is positive, then the graph of f'(x) will be above the x-axis

## Second Derivative

The *second derivative* is the derivative of the derivative function. Applying the limit definition to f' instead of f tells us:
f''(x) = lim (h -> 0) ((f'(x + h) - f'(x)) / h)
Read as f double prime of x

Take the limit twice or do the power rule twice
The alternative notation of f'' is (d^2y) / (dx^2)
#SecondDerivative

## Concavity and Convexity
*The sign of f' gives the increasing vs. decreasing nature of the function.*
Squared functions tend to always increase (unless it has a negative coefficient) because any negative number squared is positive
*The sign of f'' gives the concavity/convexity*
- If f'' > 0 then the slope of f' is increasing; hence the shape is concave up/convex (the graph "holds water")
- If f'' < 0 then the slope of f' is decreasing; hence the shape is concave down (the graph "does not hold water")
	- NOTE: if there is an x in the equation then it will have a condition (like if the second derivative is 6x then it is concave up when x > 0 and down when x < 0)

Sometimes making a table can be helpful
For f(x) = x^3 + 2x
f'(x) = 3x^2 + 2
f''(x) = 6x
+ is increasing/concave up, - is decreasing/concave down

|   |   |   |   |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|x|||0|||
|f'|+|+||+|+|
|f''|-|-||+|+|
|f info|Increasing  <br>Concave down|||Increasing  <br>Concave up||

Other equation could have more significant points but this one just has 0
Concavity is just where the first derivative is increasing/decreasing, which you could find by taking the second derivative but is useful when you only have the graph
Do not confuse this for actual increasing/decreasing. That is determined by where the first derivative is positive/negative

## Acceleration
Assume that y = s(t) gives the position at time t of an object
- v(t) = dy/dt = s'(t) is the velocity at time t
- the units of v(t) are length/time
- a(t) = (d^2y)/(dt^2) = v'(t) = s''(t) provides the acceleration at time t
- the units of s''(t) are length/time^2

The second derivative of a position function is its acceleration.
#SecondDerivative 

Helpful:
If the slope of f(x) is negative, the graph of f'(x) will be below the x-axis, positive then above
All relative extreme of f(x) will become x-intercepts of f'(x)  
All points of inflection of f(x) will become relative extreme of f'(x)

The derivative usually has one less turn than the original
